panels:
CI is a practice before it is a tool: everyone integrates into a shared mainline at least daily, and the build plus tests run on every change so integration problems surface while the diff is small. Long-lived feature branches that merge after weeks are not CI even if a pipeline runs on them; trunk-based development with short-lived branches is the usual companion.

The two CDs differ only in the last gate. Continuous delivery means the main branch is always in a deployable state and releasing is a business decision; continuous deployment removes the human gate, so the test suite and progressive rollout become your only safety net. Interviewers often probe this: continuous deployment requires strong automated tests, feature flags for unfinished work, observability to catch regressions, and automated rollback. The DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore) are the standard way to measure how well a delivery pipeline works.

Order stages by cost and signal. Compilation, linting, type checks and unit tests take seconds to a few minutes and catch most defects, so they gate everything else. Security scanning usually includes SAST (static analysis of your code), dependency scanning against known CVEs, secret detection and container image scanning; SBOM generation (software bill of materials) and artifact signing are increasingly expected for supply-chain security.

Packaging happens once, after fast checks pass. Deploys to staging then run slower integration and end-to-end tests against real infrastructure. Speed tricks: dependency and build caches, parallel jobs or test sharding, running only affected tests in monorepos, and keeping the critical path short. A common rule is that feedback on a pull request should arrive in under about ten minutes. Merge queues test the combination of queued changes against the latest main, which prevents two individually green PRs from breaking main together.

A workflow file is YAML under .github/workflows/. 'on' lists the triggering events; each job runs on a fresh runner VM ('runs-on') and contains ordered steps that either 'uses' a published action or 'run' a shell command. Jobs run in parallel unless linked with 'needs', and a 'strategy.matrix' fans one job out over versions or operating systems.

The flow-style YAML on the page is equivalent to the usual block style. Practical details interviewers like: pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA rather than a mutable tag to resist supply-chain attacks; set a minimal 'permissions' block because the default GITHUB_TOKEN may be broader than needed; store credentials in encrypted secrets, or better, use OIDC federation to obtain short-lived cloud credentials without storing keys at all. Use 'actions/cache' or setup actions' built-in caching for dependencies, and 'concurrency' groups to cancel superseded runs on the same branch.

The principle is 'build once, deploy many'. An artifact should be immutable and uniquely identified: a container image referenced by digest (sha256:...) is stronger than a tag, because tags such as 'latest' or even 'v1.2' can be moved. Tagging with the git commit SHA links every running version back to source.

Environment differences belong in configuration injected at deploy time (environment variables, config maps, secret stores), not baked into separate builds; this is the twelve-factor 'strict separation of config'. Builds should be reproducible: pin base images and lock dependency versions so the same commit yields the same output. Artifact repositories (container registries, package repositories) need retention policies, vulnerability scanning and access control. Supply-chain frameworks like SLSA add provenance attestations that record which source and builder produced an artifact, and signing tools let deploy targets refuse anything unsigned.

Rolling updates are the default in Kubernetes Deployments; maxSurge and maxUnavailable control how many extra or missing pods are allowed during the swap. They need no extra capacity, but for a while old and new versions serve traffic together, so APIs and schemas must be backward compatible.

Blue-green needs double capacity briefly but gives an instant, atomic switch and an equally instant rollback, often at the load balancer or DNS level (DNS switches are slowed by TTL caching). Canary releases shift a small share of traffic, compare error rate and latency of the canary against the baseline, and ramp in steps such as 1%, 5%, 25%, 100%; tools can automate the analysis and abort. Feature flags decouple deploy from release and allow targeting by user, region or percentage. Flags carry debt: remove them once rolled out, because stale flags multiply untested code paths.

Measure rollback by time to restore service, one of the DORA metrics. The fastest rollbacks are traffic operations (switch back to blue, set canary weight to zero, flip a flag) rather than new builds. Redeploying the previous artifact is next best, which is why keeping old artifacts and their configuration matters. 'Roll forward' with a quick fix is sometimes chosen, but only when the fix is small and the pipeline is fast.

Databases are the hard part, because data changes do not roll back. The expand/contract (parallel change) pattern splits a breaking migration into safe steps: add the new column or table, deploy code that writes both and reads new, backfill, switch reads, then later drop the old column. At every step both the current and previous app versions work against the schema. Automated rollback triggers, tied to SLO burn or canary analysis, remove human reaction time from the loop.

Flaky tests are corrosive because they destroy trust in the signal: once 'just rerun it' becomes normal, real failures get rerun too. Track flake rates, quarantine flaky tests out of the blocking path, and assign owners to fix them.

Slow pipelines change behavior. If a build takes 45 minutes, developers batch changes, and larger batches mean harder debugging and riskier releases. Secrets leak through echo statements, debug logging, verbose tool output, artifact contents and fork pull requests that can read secrets; use masked secrets, least-privilege tokens and OIDC instead of long-lived keys. Other common issues: manual steps hidden in a runbook, environment-specific builds, pipelines defined only in a web UI instead of versioned code, missing timeouts that let hung jobs block runners, and no ownership when main is red. The rule 'fix or revert main immediately' keeps everyone integrating on green.

A canary at 4% errors versus 0.5% on stable is an eightfold regression, far beyond noise, so the right call is to halt promotion and route canary traffic back to zero. Investigate afterwards with the canary's logs, traces and the diff between versions.

Nuances interviewers probe: compare the canary against a baseline running at the same time, not against historical numbers, because traffic patterns change by hour. With very small canary traffic, error rates are noisy, so require a minimum request count or a statistical test before deciding. Watch segment-specific effects: a canary may look fine overall but fail for one region, client version or request type. Finally, check that the canary and stable fleets get comparable traffic; sticky sessions or header-based routing can send unusual users to the canary and bias the comparison.
swe-devops-01.further: Next steps: trunk-based development and merge queues; the DORA metrics and the research behind them; progressive delivery tooling for Kubernetes (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) and service-mesh traffic splitting; feature flag management and flag cleanup practices; supply-chain security with SBOMs, SLSA provenance and artifact signing; OIDC federation from CI to cloud providers; and database migration tooling that supports expand/contract changes. Reading on release engineering and incident reviews shows how teams pick between rollback and roll forward under pressure.

panels:
The pyramid is a cost model, not a law. Unit tests are cheap to write, run in milliseconds and point to the exact broken function; end-to-end tests exercise real wiring but are slow, expensive to maintain and fail for reasons unrelated to your change. Hence the shape: many fast tests at the bottom, few slow ones at the top.

Alternatives exist. The 'testing trophy' popular in frontend work emphasizes integration tests, because component logic often lives in the interaction between pieces; microservice teams add contract tests between services. What matters is the ratio of confidence to cost. The ice-cream cone anti-pattern, with mostly manual or UI tests, gives slow feedback and flaky builds. A useful heuristic: test each behavior at the lowest level where it can be observed, and reserve E2E tests for critical user journeys such as signup, login and checkout.

Definitions vary by team, so clarify in interviews. A common rule: a unit test touches no network, disk, database or clock, so it is deterministic and fast; anything crossing a process boundary is an integration test. Some teams call a test of a whole module with real collaborators a unit test as long as it is fast and isolated from external systems.

Integration tests are most valuable at real boundaries: SQL queries against a real database engine (an in-memory substitute may accept queries production rejects), serialization, message queues. Containers spun up per test run make this practical. Contract tests check that a consumer and a provider agree on an API without running both. E2E tests drive a browser or API client through the deployed system; keep them few, independent and resilient, using stable selectors instead of brittle CSS paths and explicit waits instead of fixed sleeps.

The vocabulary comes from Gerard Meszaros's xUnit patterns. Stubs supply indirect inputs (return values); mocks verify indirect outputs (expected calls) and fail the test if those calls do not happen; spies record calls for later assertions; fakes are real working implementations with shortcuts, like an in-memory repository; dummies only fill parameter lists.

Trade-offs matter more than names. Heavy mocking couples tests to implementation details: refactor the internals and tests break even though behavior is unchanged. Prefer state verification (check the result) over interaction verification (check the calls) unless the call is the behavior, such as sending an email or charging a card. A common guideline is 'do not mock what you do not own': wrap third-party APIs in your own thin adapter, mock or fake the adapter, and cover the adapter itself with a few integration tests. In Python, unittest.mock with autospec catches calls with wrong signatures.

TDD's value is design pressure and fast feedback: writing the test first forces you to define the interface and expected behavior before implementation, and code written to be tested tends to have smaller units and fewer hidden dependencies. Keep steps tiny; the 'simplest code that passes' can even be a hardcoded value, which the next test then forces you to generalize (triangulation).

Refactoring is the step people skip, and skipping it produces a pile of passing but messy code. Two schools differ: classicist (Detroit) TDD uses real collaborators and verifies state; mockist (London) TDD designs outside-in with mocks for collaborators. Evidence on productivity is mixed, but TDD reliably yields a regression suite. It fits well-understood logic and bug fixes (write a failing test that reproduces the bug first); it fits less well for exploratory spikes or UI layout, where you may write tests after learning what to build.

pytest discovers files named test_*.py or *_test.py and functions prefixed test_, and rewrites plain assert statements so failures show the compared values. parametrize generates one independent test per tuple, and each appears separately in the report with an ID like test_add[2-3-5], so one failing case does not hide the others.

Fixtures are pytest's core feature: functions decorated with @pytest.fixture provide setup and teardown via dependency injection by argument name, with scopes (function, module, session) controlling reuse. Built-in fixtures include tmp_path for temporary directories and monkeypatch for safely replacing attributes or environment variables. Useful flags: -x stops at the first failure, -k filters by name, -q is quiet, --lf reruns last failures, and pytest-xdist's -n auto runs tests in parallel (which exposes hidden shared state). Use pytest.raises for expected exceptions and pytest.approx for floating-point comparisons, since 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.

Line coverage counts executed lines; branch coverage counts whether each decision went both ways; condition and MC/DC coverage go further and are required in safety-critical domains like avionics. Even perfect branch coverage cannot show that the assertions check the right things.

Goodhart's law applies: once coverage is a target, people write assertion-free tests that execute code without verifying it. Mutation testing is the stronger check: a tool introduces small bugs (flip a comparison, change a constant) and verifies that some test fails; surviving mutants reveal weak tests. Practical guidance: look at coverage diffs on pull requests to spot untested new code, set a floor to prevent decline rather than chasing 100%, and exclude generated code. Coverage around 70-90% is common in healthy projects, but the uncovered parts matter more than the number: error handling and edge cases are where bugs hide.

Root causes cluster into a few families. Timing: fixed sleeps and races with async work; wait on an explicit condition with a timeout instead. Order dependence: tests that rely on state left by earlier tests; randomize test order to reveal them. Shared state: global variables, shared databases, fixed ports, the same temp file. External dependencies: real network calls, third-party sandboxes, DNS. Time and locale: tests that fail at midnight, at month end, during daylight-saving changes or in another time zone; inject a clock. Randomness: unseeded random data. Resource limits: parallel CI runners with less CPU or memory.

Process matters as much as fixes. Detect flakes by rerunning failures and recording pass-after-retry as a flake, not a pass. Quarantine flaky tests out of the blocking path with an owner and deadline, because automatic retries alone hide real intermittent bugs, including genuine race conditions in production code.

Calling a real payment API from the main suite makes failures depend on network, rate limits and the provider's sandbox health, so the test measures their reliability instead of your code. Replace the client with a fake or stub behind your own adapter interface; then unit tests can also simulate declines, timeouts and malformed responses, which are hard to trigger on demand against a real service.

You still need some evidence that your adapter matches the real API. Options: a small set of integration tests against the provider's sandbox run on a schedule rather than on every commit, consumer-driven contract tests, or recorded responses refreshed periodically. Also make retries and idempotency keys part of the design, so a timed-out charge is not repeated twice. The key interview point: isolate the unreliable dependency at a boundary you own and test the boundary separately.
swe-devops-02.further: Explore property-based testing (Hypothesis in Python) that generates inputs to find edge cases; mutation testing to measure suite quality; consumer-driven contract testing for microservices; snapshot and approval testing, with their pitfalls; testcontainers for real dependencies in integration tests; fuzzing for parsers and security-sensitive code; and test architecture patterns such as hexagonal (ports and adapters) design that make code testable. Michael Feathers's work on legacy code shows how to add tests to code that was not written with them.

panels:
Monitoring answers known questions (is CPU high?); observability is the ability to ask new questions about system state from its outputs without shipping new code. The three signal types trade cost for detail. Metrics are pre-aggregated numeric time series (counters, gauges, histograms): cheap to store and fast to query, ideal for alerting, but they lose per-request detail. Logs are discrete events with arbitrary context, expensive at scale. Traces record causal, timed paths of single requests across services and are usually sampled.

The pillars framing is a simplification: the signals are most useful when linked. Exemplars attach a trace ID to a metric data point, so you can jump from a latency spike to a concrete slow request. Many practitioners advocate wide structured events, one rich record per request with many fields, from which metrics can be derived. Profiles (continuous CPU and memory profiling) are often called a fourth signal.

Structured logs turn text search into queries: with fields like level, service, route, status and latency_ms you can filter, group and aggregate. Use a consistent schema across services, ideally following OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, and include correlation fields: trace_id and span_id link logs to traces, and request or user identifiers (hashed if sensitive) link events from one session.

Levels need discipline: ERROR should mean something needs attention, not a handled user mistake. Logging cost is real: high-volume DEBUG logs in production can cost more than the service itself, so use sampling, dynamic levels and retention tiers. Never log secrets, tokens, passwords or full payment data, and treat personal data under privacy rules such as GDPR, with redaction at the source. Log lines should be single-line JSON written to stdout in containerized environments, letting the platform collect and ship them. Avoid logging inside tight loops.

The four golden signals come from Google's SRE book and suit request-serving systems. Two related checklists: RED (rate, errors, duration) for services, and USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources such as CPU, disks and queues.

Latency details matter. Measure successful and failed requests separately, because fast errors make average latency look better. Use histograms and percentiles: p50 shows typical experience, p99 shows the slowest 1%, and with fan-out the tail dominates; a page that calls 100 backends will hit some backend's p99 on most loads. Percentiles cannot be averaged across hosts, so aggregate histograms first. Errors include explicit failures (HTTP 5xx), wrong content returned with 200, and policy failures such as responses slower than the SLO threshold. Saturation is the leading indicator: queue length and memory pressure usually rise before latency breaks.

A good SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events, measured as close to the user as possible, e.g. at the load balancer or the client: 'proportion of HTTP requests answered successfully in under 300 ms'. Choose few SLIs per user journey: availability, latency, and sometimes freshness or correctness for data pipelines.

SLOs set a target over a window, typically 28 or 30 rolling days. 100% is the wrong target: users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% through their own networks, and every extra nine costs exponentially more. Each nine shrinks allowed downtime tenfold: per 30 days, 99% allows 7.2 hours, 99.9% 43.2 minutes, 99.99% about 4.3 minutes. SLAs are contracts with customers and include remedies such as service credits, so they are set below the internal SLO to leave a safety margin. Dependencies cap you: a service depending serially on two 99.9% services cannot exceed about 99.8%.

The error budget turns reliability into a quantity both product and engineering can spend. Request-based budgets are often better than time-based ones: with 99.9% over 10 million requests, the budget is 10,000 failed requests, and partial outages consume it in proportion to the traffic affected.

Burn rate is the key alerting concept: how fast you consume budget relative to the rate that would exhaust it exactly at window end. A burn rate of 1 uses the budget in 30 days; 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. The SRE workbook recommends multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts, e.g. page when the 1-hour burn rate exceeds 14.4 and the 5-minute window confirms it is still happening; open a ticket for slow burns. An error budget policy, agreed in advance, says what happens on exhaustion: release freezes except for reliability fixes, postmortems, and prioritizing reliability work.

A span records a name, start and end times, attributes, events and status, plus its trace ID and parent span ID; spans form a tree. Context propagation is what makes traces distributed: the W3C Trace Context traceparent header carries version, 32-hex trace ID, 16-hex parent span ID and flags, and must be forwarded across HTTP calls, message queues and async jobs; one hop that drops it breaks the trace.

OpenTelemetry is the CNCF standard: APIs and SDKs per language, auto-instrumentation for common frameworks, the OTLP wire protocol, and the Collector that receives, processes (batching, redaction, sampling) and exports to any backend. Sampling controls cost. Head sampling decides at the root, e.g. keep 10%, which is cheap but may drop the rare slow or failing requests. Tail sampling waits until the trace completes and keeps all errors and slow traces, at the cost of buffering in the collector.

Symptom-based alerting pages on what users experience, so one alert covers many possible causes, including ones nobody predicted. Cause-based alerts (high CPU, one replica down) are often not urgent thanks to redundancy and autoscaling, and they wake people for nothing. A good page is urgent, actionable, and requires human judgment; anything else should be a ticket or a dashboard.

Each alert should link a runbook with likely causes, diagnostic queries and mitigation steps, plus the relevant dashboard. Tune thresholds with 'for' durations to avoid flapping, and group related alerts so one incident does not send fifty pages. Review alerts after each on-call shift: delete any that fired without needing action. Dashboards should tell a story top-down: user-facing SLIs and golden signals first, then per-dependency panels, then resource details. Keep dashboards as code so they are reviewed and consistent across services.

Averages mislead: if 99% of requests take 50 ms and 1% take 5 s, the mean is about 100 ms and looks healthy while one user in a hundred waits. Use percentiles and histograms.

Cardinality is the number of unique label combinations, and each combination is a separate time series. A label like user_id, request ID or full URL with IDs can create millions of series, crashing the metrics backend or exploding the bill; put such identifiers in logs or traces, and keep metric labels bounded (route templates like /orders/{id}, status class, region). Alert fatigue is a safety problem: teams paged constantly start ignoring pages, and the real incident is missed. Other traps: no correlation IDs, clocks out of sync across hosts making timelines wrong, dashboards nobody owns, telemetry pipelines with no monitoring of their own, and sampling that silently drops exactly the errors you need.
swe-devops-03.further: Read the Google SRE book and workbook chapters on SLOs, alerting on SLOs and being on call; learn the OpenTelemetry Collector pipeline and semantic conventions; explore exemplars and continuous profiling; compare Prometheus-style pull metrics with push-based OTLP; study incident management (incident commander role, blameless postmortems); and look at eBPF-based instrumentation that observes services without code changes. Chaos engineering exercises test whether alerts and dashboards actually catch failures.

panels:
IaC applies software engineering practice to infrastructure: version control gives history and blame, pull requests give review, CI gives automated validation, and the same code recreates environments for testing or disaster recovery. It eliminates snowflake servers, configured by hand and impossible to reproduce.

The landscape has layers. Provisioning tools create cloud resources (Terraform and its open-source fork OpenTofu, AWS CloudFormation, Azure Bicep, Pulumi with general-purpose languages, AWS CDK which synthesizes CloudFormation). Configuration management tools configure what runs on machines (Ansible, Chef, Puppet), less central now that immutable images and containers dominate. Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts declare workloads. Immutable infrastructure is the related principle: replace servers with new images rather than patching them in place, so every running instance matches a known build. Policy as code (Open Policy Agent, Sentinel) can then check plans automatically before apply.

Declarative tools hold a desired state and a reconciliation engine computes the difference from actual state, so the same file serves for creation, update and deletion. Idempotency follows: applying unchanged code produces no changes. Imperative scripts encode a sequence of actions and must handle 'already exists' and partial failure themselves; run twice, a naive script creates duplicates.

The boundary is blurry. Pulumi and CDK use imperative languages (loops, functions, classes) to build a declarative resource graph that an engine then reconciles. Ansible modules are mostly idempotent but playbooks run in order. Kubernetes controllers are the purest declarative model: they continuously reconcile observed state toward spec, not only when you run a command. Declarative tools struggle with ordered one-off operations such as data migrations, and deletions require care: removing a resource from code means the tool will destroy it.

terraform init installs provider plugins into .terraform, records exact versions in .terraform.lock.hcl (commit this file), configures the backend and downloads modules. terraform plan refreshes state from real APIs, then diffs against configuration; symbols are + create, - destroy, ~ update in place, and -/+ destroy-then-create replacement (or +/- with create_before_destroy). Saving with -out and applying that file guarantees you apply exactly what was reviewed; if state changed in the meantime, Terraform refuses the stale plan.

Other essentials: fmt and validate in CI; plan output posted to pull requests for review; -target for emergency partial applies only, since it bypasses the dependency graph; import blocks (Terraform 1.5+) to adopt existing resources; moved blocks to rename resources without destroying them; and -refresh-only to reconcile state with reality without changing infrastructure. Use workspaces or separate directories per environment, with separate state files.

A resource block declares one infrastructure object: the type (aws_s3_bucket) selects provider and schema, the local name (logs) is your handle, and arguments configure it. Attributes known only after creation, such as arn or id, are exported for other resources to reference, and those references build the dependency graph that orders operations and parallelizes independent ones.

Since AWS provider v4, bucket settings like versioning, encryption and lifecycle rules are separate resources (aws_s3_bucket_versioning and others) that reference the bucket. S3 bucket names are global across all accounts, so a name like acme-logs-2026 may already be taken. Other HCL building blocks: variable and output blocks, locals, data sources that read existing infrastructure, count and for_each for multiple instances (for_each with map keys is safer, since removing an item from a count list shifts indexes and recreates resources), dynamic blocks, and lifecycle settings such as prevent_destroy and ignore_changes.

State records the mapping from resource addresses to real IDs, cached attributes and dependencies; without it Terraform cannot know that aws_s3_bucket.logs is a particular existing bucket. Plans compare three things: configuration, state and refreshed reality.

Remote backends store state centrally with locking. On S3, Terraform 1.10+ supports native locking with use_lockfile = true, replacing the older DynamoDB table approach; GCS and HCP Terraform lock natively. Enable bucket versioning to recover from state corruption. State stores attribute values in plain text, including generated passwords and database connection strings, so restrict access and encrypt at rest; marking variables sensitive only hides them from output, not from state. Split state by blast radius, e.g. per environment and per component (network, data, apps), so one bad apply cannot touch everything and plans stay fast. Use terraform state mv, rm and import blocks deliberately; hand-editing state JSON is a last resort.

Modules give encapsulation: inputs are variable blocks with types, defaults and validation rules; outputs expose values such as vpc_id for callers. Every configuration is a module, the root module, and it calls child modules from local paths, Git URLs or registries.

Version constraints: '~> 5.0' allows any 5.x at or above 5.0 but not 6.0, while '~> 5.0.1' allows only 5.0.x patches. Pin modules and providers, and upgrade deliberately with a reviewed plan. Design guidance: keep modules focused on one concern, avoid thin wrappers around a single resource, avoid deep nesting that hides behavior, and avoid configuring providers inside reusable modules. Composition beats giant 'do everything' modules with dozens of feature toggles. Test modules with terraform test (built in since 1.6) or tools that apply into a sandbox account, and validate examples in CI. Public registry modules save time but deserve the same review as any dependency.

Drift arises from console hotfixes, other tools or scripts touching the same resources, provider-side defaults changing, and autoscaling or managed services modifying attributes. Detection options: scheduled plan runs that alert on non-empty diffs, terraform plan -refresh-only, or platform drift-detection features. Resolution is a choice: revert reality by applying the code, or accept the change by updating the code; for fields legitimately changed outside Terraform, such as an autoscaled desired count, use ignore_changes.

GitOps, from the CNCF OpenGitOps principles, means desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable in Git, pulled automatically by software agents, and continuously reconciled. Argo CD and Flux implement it for Kubernetes; pull-based agents inside the cluster mean CI never needs cluster admin credentials. Changes, and rollbacks, happen by Git commits and reverts. For cloud resources, controllers such as Crossplane or Terraform operators bring a similar reconcile loop beyond Kubernetes.

The plan is the safety mechanism, so the most expensive mistakes come from not reading it. Replacement (-/+) of a database, load balancer or DNS record can mean data loss or downtime; changing an immutable argument, renaming a resource without a moved block, or switching count indexes are common triggers. Guard critical resources with lifecycle prevent_destroy and enable provider-side deletion protection.

State mishandling is the other big family: local state lost with a laptop, two engineers applying at once without locking, state committed to Git with secrets inside. Secrets should come from a secret manager or be generated, never hardcoded, and remember they still land in state. Other pitfalls: unpinned providers so a new major version changes behavior; one giant state for everything; long-lived drift that makes every plan noisy so real changes hide in it; and broad CI credentials. Run applies only from CI with short-lived, scoped credentials.
swe-devops-04.further: Go deeper with Terraform import and moved blocks for refactoring live infrastructure; terraform test and policy as code (Open Policy Agent, Conftest, Sentinel) in CI; OpenTofu features such as state encryption; Pulumi or CDK for language-based IaC; Kubernetes operators and Crossplane for reconciliation beyond Kubernetes; immutable images built with Packer; and landing-zone patterns for multi-account cloud setups. Studying the GitOps principles and Argo CD or Flux shows how reconciliation loops replace push-based deploys.

panels:
Service models describe where the responsibility line sits. With IaaS you get VMs, disks and networks, and you own the operating system, patches, runtime and scaling logic. PaaS (Heroku-style platforms, App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service) runs your code and handles OS and scaling. SaaS is a finished application. Containers fit between: managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) still leaves you cluster and workload configuration, while serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate, Azure Container Apps) hide the nodes.

Serverless functions bill per invocation and duration, scale to zero and scale out automatically, but have limits: cold-start latency when a new instance boots, maximum execution time (15 minutes on Lambda), statelessness, and concurrency limits. Cost crossover matters: for steady high traffic, always-on instances are often cheaper than per-request pricing; for spiky or low traffic, serverless wins. Vendor lock-in rises as you move up the stack.

Regions are independent geographic deployments, usually containing three or more availability zones; zones are physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by low-latency links (typically single-digit milliseconds), so synchronous replication across zones is practical. Names differ: AWS us-east-1a, GCP europe-west1-b, Azure numbered zones 1-3. On AWS, zone letters are mapped differently per account; use zone IDs to coordinate.

Multi-AZ protects against a data-center failure and is the default recommendation for production: load balancers spread traffic, managed databases offer a synchronous standby in another zone, and object storage is replicated across zones automatically. Multi-region protects against regional outages and serves global users with lower latency, but adds asynchronous replication, conflict handling, data-residency rules and much higher cost and complexity. Recovery targets drive the choice: RTO (how fast you must recover) and RPO (how much data you can lose). Cross-zone traffic is often billed.

Mapping names helps, but the services are not identical. Compute: EC2, Compute Engine and Azure Virtual Machines differ in instance families and discount models (reserved or committed-use discounts, savings plans, spot or preemptible capacity at large discounts that can be reclaimed). Object storage (S3, Cloud Storage, Blob Storage) stores immutable objects addressed by key, scales nearly without limit, and offers storage classes from hot to archive; S3 has been strongly read-after-write consistent since 2020.

Managed relational databases (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL Database) handle backups, patching and failover; distributed options include Aurora, AlloyDB, Spanner and Cosmos DB. Functions: Lambda, Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions) and Azure Functions. Networking: an AWS VPC is regional with zonal subnets, while a GCP VPC is global with regional subnets; Azure calls it a Virtual Network (VNet). Block storage (EBS, Persistent Disk, Managed Disks) is the other storage primitive, attached to one VM.

A VPC is a logically isolated network with a private IP range in CIDR notation: 10.0.0.0/16 provides 65,536 addresses, and each /24 subnet provides 256, minus a few reserved by the provider (AWS reserves 5 per subnet). Plan ranges so they do not overlap with other VPCs or on-premises networks you may later connect.

A subnet is public if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. Private subnets reach the internet outbound through a NAT gateway (billed hourly plus per GB processed) and receive traffic only through load balancers. Firewalls come in two flavors on AWS: security groups are stateful and attached to instances, network ACLs are stateless and attached to subnets; GCP uses VPC firewall rules, Azure uses network security groups. Private endpoints let you reach managed services like object storage without crossing the internet. Connecting networks uses peering, transit gateways or VPN and dedicated links.

IAM has principals (users, groups, roles, service accounts), actions, resources and conditions. On AWS, evaluation starts from implicit deny; an explicit Allow grants access, and any explicit Deny overrides all Allows. Policies can be identity-based or resource-based (such as bucket policies), and organization-level guardrails (service control policies) cap what any account can do.

The page's statement allows only reading objects in one bucket; note the ARN uses '/*' for objects, while listing the bucket requires s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN itself without '/*', a classic gotcha. Least privilege in practice: start narrow and add from access logs or tools that analyze unused permissions, use conditions (source network, required MFA, tags), and give workloads roles: instance profiles, Kubernetes workload identity, or OIDC federation from CI. Short-lived credentials limit the damage of a leak; long-lived access keys in code repositories are among the most common causes of cloud breaches.

The model splits security of the cloud (provider) from security in the cloud (customer). The line moves with the service: on a VM you patch the OS and configure the firewall; on a managed database the provider patches the engine but you still control network exposure, users, encryption choices and backups retention; on SaaS you still own identities, access policies and your data.

Most real cloud breaches are on the customer side: misconfigured public storage, overly permissive IAM, exposed credentials, and unpatched workloads, not failures of provider hardware. Compliance follows the same split: a provider's certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS) cover its layers and are inherited only for those layers. Tools help you hold up your side: configuration scanners and security posture management, audit logs (CloudTrail, Cloud Audit Logs, Azure Activity Log), encryption with customer-managed keys, and organization-wide guardrail policies such as blocking public buckets by default.

Cloud bills grow through many small meters. Compute that runs 24/7 for dev and test is the classic leak; schedule shutdowns and delete abandoned environments. Data transfer is asymmetric: ingress is usually free, but egress to the internet, between regions and often between zones is charged per GB, so a chatty cross-zone or cross-region design can cost more than its servers. NAT gateways charge hourly plus per GB processed; routing large object-storage traffic through them instead of a free gateway endpoint is a known trap. Logging and metrics ingestion, high-cardinality metrics and long retention add up quietly, as do unattached disks, old snapshots and idle load balancers.

The discipline is called FinOps: tag every resource with owner and environment, set budgets with alerts at thresholds, review cost by tag weekly, right-size from utilization data, use autoscaling, and buy commitments only for stable baseline load.

Public buckets remain a top cause of data leaks; enable account-level public access blocks and grant access through signed URLs or a CDN with origin access control. The root account (or global admin) should have hardware or app-based MFA, no access keys, and be used only for the few tasks that require it; daily work uses federated identities with roles.

Availability pitfalls: a single-AZ database or a single NAT gateway becomes a single point of failure, and backups that were never test-restored are only hopes. Wildcards in policies ('Action': '*' or 'Resource': '*') grant far more than intended and amplify any credential leak. Others: hardcoded credentials in images or repositories, security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH or database ports, missing audit logging, no budget alerts, quotas discovered only during an incident, and assuming the provider backs up your data automatically. Many of these can be caught automatically by policy checks on IaC before deployment.
